summary: Invent distinctive YouTube channel names for ten niches, test each against YouTube, then adversarially challenge the survivors

candidates.name: Cave Wall Street
candidates.why: Stick figures are the oldest drawings there are, on cave walls; this is money and markets explained in that same language. The stick figure holding a coin reads as a cave painting, and the name is easy to say and hard to forget. "Wall Street" leans towards markets, so the tagline should say money and economics.

candidates.why: A polite everyday phrase that hides three money words: banknotes, taking notes, and interest, which is the channel's flagship topic. It sounds calm and trustworthy, promises nothing, and leaves room for any economics subject.

candidates.name: Sketches and Balances
candidates.style: pun on a familiar phrase (checks and balances)
candidates.why: "Checks and balances" with sketches in place of checks: hand-drawn explanations of bank balances, balance sheets and how things even out. Friendly and understood on first hearing.

candidates.name: Ballpoint Figures
candidates.style: pun on a familiar phrase (ballpark figures)
candidates.why: Figures drawn in pen, and figures as in numbers, with a wink at "ballpark figures". It describes the channel exactly without the word stick. One caution: a 35.6K-subscriber channel called "Ballpark Figures" sounds similar when spoken.

candidates.name: Scribble Standard
candidates.style: pun on an economics term (gold standard)
candidates.why: The gold standard, redrawn by hand. It is playful, alliterative and pleasant to say, hints at money history, and "standard" suggests quality.

candidates.name: Sketching Account
candidates.style: pun on a banking term (checking account)
candidates.why: A checking account turned into a sketching account, where "account" also means an explanation of how something works. Short, clean and bank-flavoured without sounding like advice, though the pun is quiet and could first read as an art account.

candidates.name: Drawn on Demand
candidates.style: banking phrase with a drawing double meaning
candidates.why: Cheques are "drawn on" a bank and banknotes are payable "on demand"; here it also means hand-drawn, plus the demand of supply and demand. It could be misread as a drawing-commissions service, so the tagline matters.

candidates.name: Coin Flipbook
candidates.why: A flipbook is drawing step by step, page by page, which is how the videos are made, and the coin matches the logo. Plain words that anyone can type after hearing them once.

candidates.name: Marginal Figures
candidates.style: economics term with a drawing double meaning
candidates.why: Little figures drawn in the margins of a notebook, and "marginal", the economist's favourite word (thinking at the margin). Self-deprecating and clever, best if the audience leans towards economics.

candidates.name: Monetary, My Dear
candidates.style: pun on a familiar phrase (elementary, my dear)
candidates.why: "Elementary, my dear" with money swapped in: warm, a little cheeky, and it promises that the basics will be made obvious. It has no drawing hint, so the logo would carry that.

candidates.name: Gross Domestic Pencil
candidates.style: pun on an economics term (gross domestic product)
candidates.why: GDP with a pencil in it, and the initials still spell GDP, which makes a natural nickname. The most openly jokey option; funny, but longer and less timeless than the names above.

candidates.name: Art Supply and Demand
candidates.style: overlapping phrases (art supply + supply and demand); FOUR words, over the three-word limit
candidates.why: Art supplies meet supply and demand: the whole channel in one line, and probably the name people would smile at most. Listed last only because it is four words, one more than the brief allows; the handle is 18 characters and it passes the radio test.

named.notes:
I checked 42 names in 7 batches of 6. The checker gave a verdict every time, with no UNKNOWN and no CONTROLS FAILED. 15 came back CLEAR, 20 TAKEN and 7 CROWDED. Every verdict in candidates is the one the checker printed for that exact name in my own runs.

How crowded the niche is: obscure real money terms are already gone (Stock and Foil, Counterfoil, Note of Hand, Pay the Bearer, Moneyer, Medium of Exchange, All Else Equal), and so are the neat two-word puns (Scrawl Street, Freehand Market, Pencil Mint, Thin Margins). What cleared were fresh phrases that swap a drawing word into a finance or economics phrase, so I searched hardest there.

One candidate breaks the brief: "Art Supply and Demand" is four words. It is CLEAR and I think it is one of the strongest names, so I listed it last and flagged it rather than leave it out. Remove it if the three-word limit is firm.

Three names were CLEAR but I left them out as weaker:
- "Return on Ink": reads too close to "return on investment" for an education-not-advice channel, and the printing trade already uses the phrase.
- "Hand Minted": "minted" carries NFT and "rich" overtones.
- "Bureau of Scribbles": "bureau" is hard to spell after hearing it, and the name has no money hint.

"Economy of Line" (the art term for drawing with few lines) was marked TAKEN only because of a 26-subscriber channel called "Economy Line"; the handle itself looked free. I kept it in the failed list because the checker did not clear it.

Web searches for the 11 three-word candidates and "Art Supply and Demand" turned up no existing brand, show, book or company with those names. The eight after the first four were searched in combined queries, so those results are thinner. I did not do a trademark search.

The checks are a snapshot from today, so claim the handle soon after choosing. No files were written and the repository was not touched.

challenged.notes:
Checker: I ran it myself on all 12 names in two batches of 6. Every name came back CLEAR, with no CONTROLS FAILED and no UNKNOWN.

Web search: none ran. My first WebSearch call came back saying the search limit for this turn (200 calls, shared by every agent in the workflow) was already used up. As instructed, I didn't work around it with curl, a browser or a reader service, and I didn't use WebFetch (the task allowed only the checker and web search). So step 2 (books, podcasts, companies, apps, trademarks) wasn't done for any name. The conflicts listed come only from my own knowledge (cutoff June 2026) or the proposer's note, and are marked that way.

Under the rule 'if you are unsure whether a name is safe, it does not survive', no name survives, so recommended is left empty. Most of these names failed because the check couldn't be completed, not because a conflict was found. The ranking and scores still reflect each name's merit.

Clear knock-outs whatever the web shows:
- Ballpoint Figures: easy to mishear as the 35.6K 'Ballpark Figures' channel.
- Sketching Account: heard as 'sketchy account'.
- Coin Flipbook: sounds like a gamble and like crypto, and is close to the CoinFlip Bitcoin ATM brand.
- Marginal Figures: shares its lead word with Marginal Revolution University, an economics-education YouTube brand.
- Art Supply and Demand: four words, over the brief.

Worth a web check in a follow-up run, in this order: Cave Wall Street (best on merit), Gross Domestic Pencil, Monetary, My Dear, Scribble Standard. To get web search back, the user can send a follow-up message to continue, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION.

candidates.name: On This Site Stood
candidates.style: found phrase (the opening words of a historical marker)
candidates.why: It is how roadside plaques begin: "On this site stood the ... works." It says in four plain words that something large was built here and is gone, sounds like a film title, and every episode can open on its own marker.

candidates.name: Century Plant
candidates.style: object metaphor with a double meaning
candidates.why: The century plant (an agave) grows quietly for decades, sends up one towering flower stalk, then dies, which is the logo's line exactly. "Plant" also means factory, so it reads as a great industrial works of its century. Shortest and easiest to say of the set.

candidates.name: Founded and Foundered
candidates.why: Companies are founded; ships founder (fill and sink). The name is the channel's whole premise in three words, how they were built and how they went under, without any of the worn-out words. Slightly tongue-twisting but spelled exactly as heard.

candidates.name: Another Record Year
candidates.why: The line printed on annual reports at the very top of the curve, just before the drop, so it sits right on the logo's peak. "Record" also nods to the public records the films are built from. Ominous without saying anything negative.

candidates.name: Dry Moat
candidates.why: A moat is the business term for the advantage that protects a company; a dry moat is a castle still standing with its defence gone, which is Kodak, Blockbuster and Nokia in two words. Seven letters, punchy, easy to brand.

candidates.name: Once the Largest
candidates.why: The phrase every business obituary uses: "once the largest maker of...", "once the largest employer in...". Instantly tells a viewer the subject is fallen giants, in a sober, journalistic voice.

candidates.name: Ribbon and Padlock
candidates.why: The ribbon cut on opening day and the padlock on the gate on the last one: a company's first and final object. Very visual for intros and thumbnails, and leaves room to cover any kind of company.

candidates.name: By Order of the Board
candidates.style: found phrase (closing line of official company notices)
candidates.why: The formal line that ends company notices and filings, so it points straight at the public-record source material and has a cold, cinematic ring. Note it contains "board" (not the worn-out "boardroom").

candidates.name: Pomp of Yesterday
candidates.why: From "Lo, all our pomp of yesterday / Is one with Nineveh and Tyre", a poem about great powers passing. Elegant and serious, and says faded grandeur without any of the overused words.

candidates.name: Here Once Stood
candidates.why: A shorter sibling of "On This Site Stood" with the same marker feel; YouTube's search returned only one loosely related channel for it. Choose one of the two, not both.

candidates.name: Slipway and Seabed
candidates.why: The slipway is where a ship is built and launched; the seabed is where a lost one ends up. Built and collapsed told as two places, with zero channels of any similar name on YouTube.

candidates.name: Nine Hundred Camels
candidates.why: Legend says that when the fallen Colossus of Rhodes was finally sold for scrap, it took nine hundred camels to carry the bronze away. Unforgettable and fully ownable, with a ready-made origin story; the one weakness is that a listener might type "900".

named.notes:
42 names checked in 7 runs; the checker never printed CONTROLS FAILED or UNKNOWN. 15 came back CLEAR and 12 are listed, best first.

Three CLEAR names were dropped as weak:
- Receiver of Wreck: it is the title of a real UK government official, so it could cause confusion.
- Agate Type: too oblique; it does not hint at the subject.
- Sold for Scrap: reads like a scrap-metal channel and covers only the ending.

What the failures showed:
- Accounting and filing terms are crowded by this exact niche. "Material Weakness" has six channels, one subtitled "How Companies Fall Apart", and "Substantial Doubt" and "The Registrant" are gone too.
- Short technical terms and single rare words are almost always taken as handles (Falsework, Strandline, Index Fossil, Top of Descent, Hammer Price).
- Famous poem lines are taken ("Look On My Works", "Nothing Beside Remains").
- What cleared were found phrases from markers, annual reports and notices, and unexpected pairings of two objects or places.

Limits of the check:
- Verdicts cover YouTube handles and channel names only. No trademark, domain or other social-platform check was done.
- A web search for existing podcasts, books or brands was run on six names (On This Site Stood, Century Plant, Dry Moat, Founded and Foundered, Another Record Year, By Order of the Board) and found none. The other six listed names did not get that search.
- Handles are shown as the checker tested them; YouTube handles are not case-sensitive.
- "Century Plant" is also the common name of an agave, so a plain web search for it returns plant results; no channel has the name.
